own_scenes.desc: Bajo la presión de la guerra, el centro se erosionaba. Frente a la cultura juvenil cada vez más segura y hostil, los adultos y los conservadores empujaron con todas sus fuerzas: George Wallace usó el country en 1964 y Ronald Reagan anunció en enero de 1966 su candidatura a gobernador de California prometiendo no dejar que una «minoría ruidosa y disidente» pusiera de rodillas a una gran universidad.

notes.chapter: Octubre: Winchester Cathedral: tiempo pasado, presente y futuro
notes.text: En otoño de 1966 Ronald Reagan iba en la cresta de la ola: contra el crimen, la inmoralidad de los «beatniks, radicales y defensores del lenguaje obsceno» de Berkeley y los disturbios, por la ley, el orden, el patriotismo y los negocios sin trabas. No hablaba por los jóvenes sino por sus padres, que no entendían por qué sus hijos no querían ser carne de cañón en una guerra no declarada ni por qué los negros pedían más. Su equipo veía con buenos ojos que los disturbios volvieran antes de las elecciones.

notes.chapter: Noviembre: Good Vibrations: Motown y el soul en Reino Unido, los Beach Boys y el Sunset Strip
notes.text: El 8 de noviembre Ronald Reagan ganó el gobierno de California y los republicanos resurgieron en todo el país: para el historiador Andrew E. Busch, la Gran Sociedad acabó en las elecciones de 1966 y empezó la era moderna de la fuerza republicana. Reagan había explotado el miedo blanco y apuntado a Berkeley; a Mario Savio le negaron la readmisión. La iniciativa CLEAN contra la obscenidad (Proposición 16) perdió, pero dio cobertura a la policía de San Francisco para detener el 15 de noviembre al dependiente de la Psychedelic Shop y después al de City Lights por vender The Love Book de Lenore Kandel.

influences.name: Discos de respuesta y country patriótico

refs.q: The New Right was on the march.
refs.para: The New Right was on the march. Stimulated by editorials that described the Berkeley protests as a ‘nightmarish carnival’, the Republican politician Ronald Reagan moved to make student unrest a central plank of his campaign for the governorship of California. In the January 1966 announcement of his candidacy, Reagan posed a question that concealed a threat: ‘Will we allow a great university to be brought to its knees by a noisy, dissident minority?’

refs.q: In autumn 1966, Reagan was on the crest of a wave.
refs.para: In autumn 1966, Reagan was on the crest of a wave. He was a sharp, elusive operator, cannily avoiding questions about his right-wing affiliations while promoting a classic laissez-faire agenda. He directly addressed public concerns about the apparently unravelling social fabric, speaking out passionately against rising crime levels, moral turpitude – epitomised by the ‘beatniks, radicals and filthy speech advocates’ at the University of California, Berkeley – and the riots that seemed to be spreading through the cities of the state. Reagan stood for old-fashioned values: the right of business to be unimpeded, the rule of law and order and, above all, patriotism. In his eyes, student protestors were, quite simply, un-American and treasonous. He did not speak for the young but for their parents, the large number of middle-aged Americans who had either served or lived through the war, and had participated in the country’s great expansion during the 1950s. This generation could not understand why a section of their young did not want to offer themselves as cannon fodder for an undeclared war.

refs.q: There was trouble in paradise. On 8 November, Ronald Reagan was elected as the governor of California
refs.para: There was trouble in paradise. On 8 November, Ronald Reagan was elected as the governor of California by just under 100,000 votes. The result was a major reversal for the Democrats, who had held the state for eight years, but, even more so, it signified a major shift in American politics. ‘Republican Resurgence’, trumpeted Time magazine: apart from eight governorships – which increased their tally to twenty-five out of fifty in total – the GOP won 700 seats in state legislatures, compared to the party’s 529-seat loss just two years previously.

refs.q: The forces of contraction were embodied that day in two vice squad detectives called Peter Maloney and Sol Weiner.
refs.para: The forces of contraction were embodied that day in two vice squad detectives called Peter Maloney and Sol Weiner. At 2.30 p.m., they entered the Psychedelic Shop on 1535 Haight and bought a copy of the recently published The Love Book by Lenore Kandel. Fetching two uniformed officers from the street, they arrested the shop’s clerk, Allen Cohen, for selling an obscene work. They closed the shop and began harassing the customers. Another young man, James Helms, was arrested when he tried to force his way in.
